title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Intestinal Parasitic Infections Among Internally Displaced Persons in Karary Locality, Sudan: A Cross-Sectional Study
content: Intestinal parasitic infections (IPIs) represent a significant public health challenge in displaced populations, where overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, limited access to safe water, and compromised healthcare services facilitate faecal-oral transmission. This study determined the prevalence of intestinal parasitic infections and evaluated demographic, displacement-related, hygiene, water, and behavioural factors associated with infection among internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Karary Locality, Sudan. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 250 internally displaced persons residing in temporary settlements and camps in Karary Locality. Fresh stool specimens were collected and examined using direct wet-mount microscopy with 0.9% physiological saline at x10 and x40 magnifications for the identification of protozoan cysts, trophozoites, and helminth eggs. Structured interviews were administered to gather data on demographic characteristics, duration of displacement, prior parasitic infection history, water sources, sanitation access, and hygiene practices. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 27 using descriptive statistics and chi-square test for categorical comparisons. Intestinal parasitic infections were identified in 81 of the 250 participants (32.4%). Giardia lamblia was the most prevalent species (40/250, 16.0%), followed by Entamoeba histolytica (13/250, 5.2%), Entamoeba coli (13/250, 5.2%), and Hymenolepis nana (5/250, 2.0%). Strongyloides stercoralis, Enterobius vermicularis, and Ascaris lumbricoides were each detected in 1 participant (0.4%), while mixed infections occurred in 7 participants (2.8%). Infection prevalence was significantly associated with age group (p=0.043), with the highest proportion of cases occurring among children aged 5–14 years (32/81, 39.5%), and duration of displacement (p< 0.001). Conversely, no statistically significant associations were detected between infection status and sex, prior history, water sources, hygiene practices, or health education exposure. Intestinal parasitic infections affected nearly one-third of the evaluated IDP population in Karary Locality, predominantly driven by protozoan species like Giardia lamblia. Age and duration of displacement were key correlates, highlighting the urgent need for targeted interventions prioritizing safe water supply, improved sanitation, hygiene education, and accessible treatments in IDP settlements.
